title: Release notes a customer will read
excerpt: Open a release note with what the customer can do now, where it lives, and who it is for. Put the ticket number at the end, or leave it in the tracker.
alt: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table, a surface where the thing a person can do now has to earn the first line.
caption: A phone full of app icons. Lead the note with what the customer can do now. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should a release note start?
faqs.answer: Start with the new ability, in a sentence you would say on a call, plus where it is and who it is for. A version number can sit at the end if someone must search for it. Excitement about the team's effort spends the only sentence many people will read.

faqs.question: Where should internal ticket numbers go?
faqs.answer: At the end of the note, in a quiet line, or in the admin view. They help a support agent and the person who filed the request. They should not be the heading. Translate technical causes into what the customer experienced, or leave them out.

faqs.question: What should you leave out of public release notes?
faqs.answer: Changes you might revert next week, features that are not in the product today, and price changes buried in a last line. Also skip refactors that do not change the customer's day. Those belong in the internal log, so the public channel stays worth opening.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Release notes should open with what the customer can do now. The new verb, the place in the product, and who it is for. A ticket number, a squad name, and a list of files changed can sit at the end, or they can stay in the tracker. Release notes ux writing is the choice to lead with the customer's new ability instead of the team's effort.

If the customer can do nothing new, you may not need a note. A refactor that does not change their day can live in the internal log. Publishing it as news trains people to ignore the channel you will need later.

## The first sentence is the ability

Write the ability the way you would say it to a customer on a call. "You can assign an overdue order without leaving the list." "You can download the month as a file your bookkeeper already opens." That sentence is the note. Everything else is support.

Name the person when the ability is not for everyone. "Admins can require a second approver on refunds." A note that hides the role will generate questions from people who cannot see the control, and they will think the product is broken. The role is part of the news.

Say where it is. "On the orders list, open the row." One location. If it is in two places, say the one you want them to use. A tour of the information architecture does not belong in the first line.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on how long people stay is the editing tool. Users often leave in 10 to 20 seconds, and they read only about a quarter of the text. Your first sentence may be the only sentence. It has to contain the ability. A preamble about "listening to feedback" spends the window on you.

Keep the title the same kind of sentence, shorter. Google's guidance on title links asks for descriptive, concise titles, and for a main heading that is clearly the main heading. "Assign overdue orders from the list" works as both. "Release 4.3.1" does not, unless your readers are the people who ship it. You can put the version at the end of the title if someone must search for it. Do not let the version be the only words.

## What comes after the sentence

The picture, if the control is hard to picture. A tight crop, with the new thing visible, and alt text that repeats the ability for someone who cannot see the crop. A full-window screenshot at low contrast will be skipped. The picture is a second copy of the first sentence, not a mood.

The limit, in one line, if there is a limit. Plan, role, region, or a case you do not handle yet. Limits in the second paragraph prevent a delighted forward from turning into a support ticket. Hide the limit and you have written an ad.

The step, if there is one step. If there are six, link to the guide. The note is not the manual. A migration, in particular, needs its own page with the order, the breakage, and the time. Link it. Do not compress a migration into a cheerful paragraph. People will try to follow the paragraph and get stuck.

The date, if the date matters. "Available now." "Available 4 May." "Rolling out this week." If the rollout is partial, say so. "You will see this when it reaches your workspace" is honest. "Available now" while half the customers cannot see it is how trust erodes in a channel that is supposed to create trust.

Skip the origin story. Who requested it, how long you worked, and how proud the team is can be a single quiet line if a specific customer is waiting to feel seen. It is a poor second sentence. The second sentence should help the next action.

## Internal detail, at the end or nowhere

The ticket number helps a support agent and a champion who filed the request. Put it at the end, in a quiet line, or in the admin view of the note. Do not make "Fixes HB-1844" the heading. The customer does not dream in your tracker.

The technical cause belongs in the note only when the customer felt the cause. "The export no longer drops the last row" is a customer sentence. "Resolved an off-by-one in the pagination helper" is an internal sentence. Translate it. If you cannot translate it into something they experienced, ask whether the note is for them.

Group fixes after the abilities, under a plain heading. "Also fixed." Short lines, customer language, no puzzle. A crash they saw. A number that was wrong. A mail that did not send. If you have twenty fixes, you may publish the ones customers reported and keep the rest internal. A wall of fixes teaches people that your product is a list of wounds. A short list teaches them you noticed.

Security fixes need care. Say that you fixed a vulnerability if users must act, and say the action. Do not publish a recipe. If they must do nothing, a brief line may still be right for trust, reviewed by the person who owns security. When you are unsure, write less and give a path to ask. The security page is where the standing facts live. The note is where the change lives.

Do not change the date of an old note to make the product look freshly updated. Google's helpful-content guidance treats false freshness as a warning sign. A new ability earns a new note. An old note keeps its date. If the ability changed, add a line to the old note or write a new one that links back. Do not pretend March was June.

## A format a small team will keep

Use one template. Title as the ability. One paragraph. Optional picture. Optional limit. Optional link. Date. Quiet ticket line. A template is how notes get published on the day, instead of saved as a draft until the launch feeling has passed.

Give the template an owner, and give the owner a backup. The person who merged the change is often the wrong sole author, because they are deep in the internal name. A second pass by someone who talks to customers will restore the verb. On a small team that pass can be ten minutes. Skip it and the note will say "pagination helper."

Publish where the customer already is. A page on the site, a panel in the product, or both, with the same words. Two versions will diverge by Friday. Pick a source. Hanabi would rather the words live in the product's content, editable, than in a social post that disappears. The marketing site can link to the current set. It should not invent a second adjective for the same ability.

Keep the voice of the product. Short sentences. The verb on the button. If the product says "Assign," the note says "Assign." A launch voice that appears only in notes feels like a different company, the same way a campaign page feels wrong when it invents a second brand. You can be warm. You do not need a drumroll.

Read the last five notes as a set. If every one opens with "We are excited," you have a tic, and the ability is buried. Delete the tic from the template so the next author does not have to be brave.

## What not to announce

Do not announce a change you might revert next week. Wait until you would let a customer plan a workflow on it. A note is a small contract. Breaking it casually makes the next note weaker.

Do not announce a feature that is a logo on a slide. If it does not exist in the product today, it is not a release. It is a roadmap item, and roadmap items belong in a conversation with their own uncertainty labeled. The integrations page has the same rule. What actually works, what it does, what it does not.

Do not announce a price change inside a feature note as a surprise in the last line. Money gets its own sentence, its own page if the shape changed, and enough time for a buyer to see it. Mixing it into "also, we cleaned up the header" is how a company looks like it is sneaking.

Do not use the notes to scold customers for using the product wrong. If a behavior changes, say what to do now. "The old export is gone. Use Download month" is a direction. "We removed the old export because nobody should have used it" is a slight. You can be clear without it.

Wabisabi, Ballarat Box Sports, and the product interfaces in Hanabi's public work all depend on a stable voice. Release notes are part of that voice, even when a studio is writing them for a client's product. They are not a side channel for leftover personality.

## Where the notes sit in the product

Let a signed-in customer see what changed since their last visit, if you can do it without a carnival. A quiet list, newest first, the ability as the link. Unread is useful. A modal that blocks the product until they click through is not useful. They came to do the job. The note is a courtesy.

Let a prospective customer see a public subset, if the abilities help them decide. Strip the ticket numbers. Keep the limits. A public changelog full of internal codes looks like a product in distress, even when the news is good. Edit for the reader who is not in your Slack.

Keep old notes findable. A buyer checking whether you fixed the export in April should find April. Do not collapse history into one evergreen page that rewrites the past. History is the point of the genre.

If a note describes a flow that takes something away, a plan, a permission, a habit, say what they keep and what they lose, and let them act. The piece on [an honest cancellation flow](/blog/designing-a-cancellation-flow-that-is-honest) is the next read when the "new ability" is actually an ending. Endings deserve the same plain sentence as launches.

To see work that leads with the job rather than the machinery, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). A release note should be that direct. The customer can do this now. The rest is optional.
